utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I could remind you of the affirmation which you took when your evidence commenced, it still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before my learned friend commences, may I just have the floor for a moment to make a correction to the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to the exhibit bearing number P160, Your Honour will recall that the Malutka, which was positioned at Hotel President in Lapad was marked as B, with the letter B. But unfortunately, in the map, it has been marked with the letter -- I'm sorry, it should have been marked with the letter D, but in the map by mistake it has been marked with the letter B. And this could lead to confusion because there are two positions with the letter B. Could that be corrected, Your Honour. Perhaps I could even do this in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you have given us notice of it. If you deal with it in re-examination, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I have one further correction. That is at page 9 in LiveNote. And the third question, actually more than transcript error, I have phrased the question incorrectly, and that does not reflect the factual situation. So may I just read it out, Your Honour. I have asked the question in this manner: "And then you added two positions to the map, being positions that were there on the 6th of December 1991, which are not reflected in this map, being the Malutka position at Hotel President in Lapad by the coursal line [sic], the position marked D, and the position at Mala Petka, which is the position marked C." But the factual situation is, Your Honour, that the witness added three positions. In addition to the positions I identified here, there is also an additional position marked A, that is, the rocket launcher close to Hotel Libertas. And I think my learned friends do not object to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you've drawn attention to it so that Mr. Rodic has notice of it, and we are aware of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Negodic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We will continue where we left off on Friday. Can you tell me whether you know that the 1st engineering group established in Dubrovnik on the 28th of July 1991 actually started operating in August the same year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the very beginning, at Beru Tana [phoen] Pobrezje, that mines were being removed -- were being placed with 45 kilograms of Vitezit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I'm just aware of the TUP factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In August, was the area of Vitalijna destroyed; and the Brgat road, was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I know part of Konavle, vis-a-vis Siroki Brijeg, but I don't know about the second question that you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the month of September was the area of Ostojnik mined?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the mining of communications between Slano and Zavala?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of September, was the hill of Palas on the Brgat Ivanica Road mined?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The ports in Gruz harbour, were they mined?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The approach to the port of Gruz.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the area at the defence line of Dubrovnik mined? That part of town that was defended?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: A detachment of armed boats formed on the 1st of September 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not get the names of the commander, the deputy commander. The speakers are too fast.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I know that it was established. But I'm not aware of the names of the commander and the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik in the month of November, was the Croatian Navy established with a commander for Dubrovnik, Nikola Plizvic [phoen] being the commander?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did speed boats bring in ammunition and weapons as well as personnel into Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me from which area they brought these supplies in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, via Peljesac, Mljet, Sipan, Lopud, Kolocep, and then the Bay of Lapad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, within logistics, are food and accommodation of personnel organised in the following way: Using hotel rooms to a maximum?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Every hotel has its own kitchen, and that was the most appropriate place for preparing food.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat. When I ask about this type of logistics, I'm asking about the Croatian Army. Were hotels used for their food and accommodation in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. Only food was prepared for the military. And the military was deployed just like my part, in Rasica, which was an abandoned recreation area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could all the defenders fit into Vila Rasica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were vehicles and drivers mobilised in Dubrovnik for military purposes from all companies and from the entire business community, mainly Dubrovkinja and DST?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After Kupari fell on the 24th of October, did the number of Croatian soldiers go down and were they abandoning Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. There were different groupings in the town of Dubrovnik, in the narrow sense of the word, so I cannot exactly tell whether the number actually changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the meeting held between Nojko Marinovic and then Eduard Cengija and Mladen Jurkovic [phoen] in the Hotel Zagreb on the 24th of October an agreement was reached to remain in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any details, but there was a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 25th of October, did Cengija and Mladen Jurkovic with their guard take the outskirts of town on the east, as well as the defence line going from Ploca to Orkanski Visovi [phoen] and the area in front of the Argentina Hotel towards Zlatni Potok?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this area was taken, the eastern area, because it was assumed that the old road [Realtime transcript read in error "town"] to Dubrovnik, the pathway, could be used for an infantry attack. I cannot tell you about any further details. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And on the same day, did the guard take the area of the road from Ploca towards Ilijina Glavica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, along the entire length of the road above town as the road goes, that is a pedestrian area, and it was covered in its entirety, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause, Mr. Rodic. Two matters in the transcript. At 5, line 15 at the moment, you refer, sir, to the town of Dubrovnik in the narrow sense of the word. If you can see the screen in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- it's now line 15. I'm talking principally to the witness at the moment. Can you see the screen in front of you, the television. You haven't a screen. Do you see line 15, you speak of Dubrovnik, the "town in the narrow sense of the word." I wondered what you were meaning there by the "the narrow sense of the word."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I say that, I mean the territory of town, except for the bordering municipalities. So I'm not talking about the Old Town only. I'm talking about the territory from Ploca to Sustjepan. That is what we consider to be the "town in the narrow sense of the word" but not referring only to the old historical centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I felt you didn't, but I thought it needed to be clarified. Can you also look at line 25. Well, I don't think you need to look; I think it should simply be noted that there is an error in the transcript. What you said in the English translation was that "it was assumed that the old road to Dubrovnik" whereas what is recorded is the Old Town. So we'll just notice that there was an error there and "town" should read "road." Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, let us clarify this once again. When you talk about the town of Dubrovnik, there is the Municipality of Dubrovnik. That is a much broader area. And the town of Dubrovnik then, and then the Old Town of Dubrovnik. In this case, when you speak of the town of Dubrovnik, and when you speak of positions in the town in the narrower sense of the word, could you tell us geographically again which -- what that area be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: When we say the town in the narrow sense of the word, I mean the road coming from Dubac, the eastern approach, that is. Then on the other side, the approach from the main road from the village of Sustjepan to the harbour of Gruz. So it is Ploca, Gruz, Lapad, et cetera. When I talk about the Old Town, allow me to say simply the Old Town. And by saying that, I will mean that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me continue in relation to these questions pertaining to the taking of positions in this town in the narrow sense of the word on the 25th of October 1991. Tell me, do you know whether on that day or in that period the special police entered the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. May I just add something. As far as I know, an order was issued for uniformed persons, soldiers and policemen alike, were not allowed to move about the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know then who issued this order that uniformed soldiers or policemen were not allowed to move about the Old Town, within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It was issued by the commander for the defence of Dubrovnik. Nojko Marinovic. That was an order issued to the subordinate officers, and they were supposed to convey these orders to their soldiers. The same goes for the police. But I don't know how this was addressed to the police, in which way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume, and you will tell me whether I'm right, that this same order probably regulated the fact that no arms were allowed in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. This order was valid in the military, and I assumed it was valid for the police, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, during the month of November, there was a reestablishment in the military formations of Dubrovnik. The 1st Battalion, was it then commanded by Eduard Cengija?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I know that he was there, but I think the commander of the 1st Battalion was the one you mentioned a few minutes ago. The same last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mladen Jurkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, Mladen Jurkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mladen Jurkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he participate in the defence of Dubrovnik all the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. But I cannot give an answer with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the command post of this battalion, was it at the dormitory for women students?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The positions of this battalion, in the month of December 1991, were they between Ilijina Glavica to Orsula and the Belvedere Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in the month of November 1991 a mixed detachment was formed of marines and landing infantry in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I just know that the navy as such was established. But what it actually boiled down to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in the month of November groups for providing security along the sea belt were established in the Croatian Navy?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, groups were established, but what units they actually consisted of, I don't know. It was like duty in the Bay of Lapad and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the area of the Splendid Hotel, was Zeljko Djuratovic the commander of such a group?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: One of these hotels. I don't know if it was Splendid or Vis. And who commanded this group, I can't say, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you for the names of these commanders. But I'll just ask you whether you know that these groups for providing security in the sea belt were by the Adriatik Komodor Hotel, the Vila Edit, Vila Elita, and the Argos Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As for these first hotels, you mentioned, yes. As for the Argos Hotel, I really don't know. These hotels, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, were in the Bay of Lapad. That's where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The command of the defence of Dubrovnik, in the month of October 1991, did it reach a decision that if and when necessary and with a view to organising defence, all houses that are on the approaches of town should be used for protection and for firing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was in oral or written form. But the houses by the road, by the front line, were used for accommodation and food and that's also where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know maybe whether that decision was approved by the executive board of the Dubrovnik Municipality towards the end of 1991, towards the end of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In case they resisted, would the owners of these houses be criminally liable? Was that the law at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But I do know that all those houses were abandoned because the owners left for security reasons. They went to hotels and big buildings that had nuclear shelters. And those buildings included the hospital, et cetera. Those houses were abandoned by the owners and their families because they were on the first defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Several times during your examination-in-chief, you said that after the landing and assault in Kupari and the fall of Kupari on the 24th of October 1991, JNA occupied Zarkovica and Bosanka on the same day or the next day? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but I said that I could not be precise to a day. It could have been the night between the 24th and the 25th or between the 25th and the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, but tell me, was that fact, the fall of Bosanka, Kupari, and Zarkovica, the reason why this defence line was established in the Dubrovnik proper, Dubrovnik in the narrow sense of the word as you put it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I served in the artillery so that I am not really aware of why it wasn't done two days earlier or two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the middle of November 1991, was the new defence line of Dubrovnik from Orsula, Belvedere Hotel, Zlatni Potok, Orkanski Visovi, Srdj Hill, Nuncijata, Sustjepan, and along the coastline from Babin Kuk, Uvala [phoen], Lapad, Gradac, Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the reserve captain, Darko Pracki [phoen] command over the 76-millimetre cannon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Ivica Santic command a 76-millimetre battery of cannons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Did you say battery of cannons? He was commander of the artillery rocket battalion in the process of being established. How can he -- how could he be a commander of a couple of cannons? A couple of cannons would form a platoon rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did Damir Golemac, a reserve lieutenant, command over a rocket launcher of 128 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. For a while, he occupied that position. But he was initially engaged as a surveyor in order to train people to use maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Hajrudin Fazlic, junior lieutenant, was he a commander of a mortar battery of 82 and 128 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: If we are talking about November and December, he was deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'll remember his name later, and I'll tell you. Oh, he was Mratovic, M-r-a-t-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Stojan Gadzic, was he a commander over the Maljutka and Tijton [phoen] weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I cannot really say that he was a commander. But he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean that he was in charge of the Maljutka anti-tank weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the area of the Ilijina Glavica, were there two cannons of 85 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In the area of the town in November and December, we did not have any 85-millimetre cannons. They were deployed in that area in October. One in the front part of Konavle. That one was captured, together with a crew. And the crew was in Morinje. The second cannon remained above the hotel in Cavtat, the Croatia Hotel, and it was abandoned by the crew facing an onslaught by the army. These were the two 82-millimetre cannons that I mentioned on Friday. You have it all on record. You mentioned four. I told you about the location of two of them. And I don't know about the other two because I had never seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's right. When we talked on Friday, I asked you about Nojko Marinovic and the fact that he brought four such cannons from the island of Korcula to Dubrovnik, and you said you knew only about two of them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the other two?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the recoilless cannon in the area of Ilijna Glavica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. The recoilless cannon as I have shown on the map was supposed to be used as an anti-artillery weapon used preventively so that ships could not enter the Gruz port. That is how I received my assignment and conveyed it further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did this recoilless cannon ever change position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. In the second half of December, that was the time when the ships that were logistical support in Slano and Zaton Bays were brought closer to the Kolocep island, and they did have sufficient range. One night we moved Maljutka to the island of Kolocep and replaced it with one of these recoilless cannons. Then negotiations ensued to prevent fire being opened on ships that were logistical ports in Slano and Zaton Bays.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that before the signing of the ceasefire on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. It was 12 or 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When there was a combat group in Ilijna Glavica with two mortars of 128 millimetres and one Maljutka, were these weapons there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any reason why anybody would put a Maljutka on Ilijna Glavica when it can serve no purpose there. It would be simply decorative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the area of Gospina Polja, were there two 66-millimetre ZIS cannons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Gospina Polja is a broader area. One 66-millimetre ZIS cannon was positioned, and another was in Mala Petka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December in Ivo Vojnovic Street, was there an exchange of fire between a unit of military police and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When several members of the brigade got killed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: During that whole day, I was in the vicinity of that street. But from what I could see, there was no misunderstanding and no commotion. And as far as that part of the street that I couldn't see is concerned, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this conflict, this clash?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some stories going around. But I was too busy doing other things, and I was also wounded on that day. So that several days after that, I ended up in hospital. So I cannot help you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it. Tell me, where were you wounded? How?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I was driving a Renault 4. An explosion threw a garbage bin at me, and I got hurt. Somebody put a compression bandage on me and some painkillers, and I was returned to my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at what time did that happen?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It could have been around 8.00 -- sorry, 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean 11.00 a.m. on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, because at half past 11.00 when I returned, I went again to this combat position, the SDK, which was out of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, that what happened when you were on your own position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, that happened when I was going towards Babin Kuk. We had a lightly injured person with us. And from the hotel in Babin Kuk, I picked up a woman who was seriously wounded, and I was driving both of them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, from your position you went to Babin Kuk, the Tirena Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. To the camp where 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre mortars were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There at Babin Kuk, you picked up some people whom you later drove to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Only one. A member of my unit, and that woman who I believe was a cleaning lady. And by the way she was bleeding, I thought that she was seriously wounded, but I cannot give you any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To what hospital did you drive them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: To Medarevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How far is that hospital from your position, the one where the cannon was in the Ivo Vojnovic street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Do you mean when you're driving a car or as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Give us the distance in kilometres, not in minutes. From the Ivo Vojnovic street to the Medarevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: A kilometre and perhaps 200 metres, 1.2 kilometres. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From your position in Ivo Vojnovic street to Babin Kuk, the Tirena Hotel and that fire position that you were touring?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: 1.5, 1.6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And where exactly were you wounded at Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: At the turnoff from Ivo Vojnovic to Medarevo hospital. That's 50 metres before the traffic light.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, did that happen when you were going there or when you were coming back?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: When I was going there. From my position, from my artillery position to Babin Kuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were hurt, and you picked up those wounded people on the way, and you were going to Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were hurt? Could you tell me in more detail?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As I was driving, I got hurt more by the power of the explosion than any shrapnel or anything. It shattered my windshield, and I was thrown out of the vehicle, literally launched out of it, and landed, crashed, against the garbage bin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, your windshield was shattered?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, the windshield was shattered, that's what I saw later. But the explosion launched me out of the car, and I crashed against a garbage bin. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you-- were you thrown out of the vehicle or did you crash together with the vehicle into that garbage bin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I was -- I crashed into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you given any medical assistance at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: They gave me -- they put a compression bandage on me and gave me some painkillers and told me that I was free to spend the night there if I felt that was necessary. But I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That compression bandage, where did they put it? Which part of your body?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That's the thoracic vertebrae, a part of my backbone that turned out to be hurt to prevent excessive movement that could cause even greater damage when I breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there any bleeding?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir. Negligible. My temple was hurt, nothing major.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you alone in the car or were there any more people?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How did you manage to drive on after such shock and trauma?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know if you will understand me when I say this, but those are very extraordinary situations. And even a person like I gets some unusual strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in terms of time, how long did it all take, your going to Babin Kuk, the explosion, the wound, going to the hospital, the medical assistance you received?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't think it took more than 40 minutes all in all because I didn't put those people in the car myself. I wasn't physically able to. Other people helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So this conflict that I asked you about in relation to the street of Ivo Vojnovic, you heard about it, but you yourself were not present. You were not nearby.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In the evening when the gunfire stopped, as it was getting dark, when I came to headquarters, I heard people talking and saying "why was this gunfire necessary?" So I was in pain, and I really didn't feel like listening to any squabbles. I don't know if this answer is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear perhaps that on that occasion fire was opened from infantry weapons and that grenades were thrown at the MUP patrol? Was that mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know, you yourself, or did you hear about any clashes in the town of Dubrovnik itself in which the members of the HOS took part?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I never even saw them. But I only know, as I've already told you, that there were supposed to be about ten of them up at Srdj. But as for a town, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a particular term, if I could tell me. What is "flak"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It's not a weapon I used. It could be used by anti-aircraft defence. But I can't really go into details. I'm not an expert in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the expression "flak" for an anti-aircraft gun or cannon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I heard of its use, but it could be used in infantry as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It's that particular weapon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I heard the expression "they fired with a flak" or something like that. Sir, may I just add one more thing by way of clarification. Perhaps sometimes you will be surprised by my answers but I'm not a professional soldier. I do not have any special fondness for weapons. What I did and what I did in the former Yugoslavia, the fact that I defended this town, as I would have defended the former Yugoslavia where I was born. I would have defended it with all my heart. I'm referring to the former Yugoslavia now. That's how I did this, too. But I repeat: I have no special fondness for arms. And after all these years, in response to your questions that are very fair, I want to answer everything I can, everything I know, and I forget these details about weapons faster than I forget details about people. Do you understand this? Can you appreciate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I fully appreciate this. But please understand me, too. I have to put many questions that have to do with professional activity, too, since you were such positions. I simply have to ask you these questions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Please go ahead, sir. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the point for mobile weapons, the 20-millimetre anti-aircraft gun, the single-barrelled gun, the so-called Erlikon, was it above the Excelsior Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was in the Gruz harbour, the Lapad Hotel, that area approximately. Now, whether they moved it from there is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You don't know perhaps whether this vehicle and weapon was partly hidden in the garage of the Excelsior Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly. Because it is a heavy-duty garage, so perhaps it could be there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear this Erlikon single-barrel gun expression? Did you ever hear of this as an expression?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I heard of it as an expression, but I wasn't really interested in hearing more about this weapon. But yes, the word itself, Erlikon, yes, it was heard often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the walls of the Old Town, was there an anti-aircraft gun, 20-millimetre, single barrelled?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no weapons of the larger calibre, at least, were ever put in the Old Town. I said during the first day when the lady was putting her questions to me, I cannot say that there were only hunting guns there, that people who escaped from Konavle and Zupa Dubrovacka brought their hunting guns and pistols, things like that. That I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, but I'm asking you something else, not about within the Old Town, but I'm asking but the fort, the ramparts, the walls of the Old Town. Do you know whether there was ever a cannon positioned there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Because the explicit order issued to all commanders was to convey to the soldiers not only for them to remain within the Old Town, but that at all costs they should avoid being even close to it. So that possibly by targeting a military objective, the Old Town would be hit. This was avoided at all costs, and every effort was made. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the Bay of Lapad, was there an anti-aircraft gun with a single barrel, 20 millimetres, but a mobile one?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As I've already said to you, I know the region approximately. It's also Lapad. What you're asking me about now and what I said to you a few minutes ago, around the Lapad Hotel. So it does face Gruz.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, there are a couple of corrections to the transcript. At page 20, line 8, because the explicit order issued to all commanders was to convoy to the soldiers, not only for them to remain within the Old Town, but that at all costs they should avoid being even close to it. I wonder whether the witness said "not to remain within the Old Town." That is one, Your Honour. And further up, line 1 of page 20, "I said during the first day when the lady was putting her questions to me, I cannot say that there were only hunting guns there." I wonder whether the witness meant to say "I can say that there were only hunting guns" because that was the evidence in chief. Perhaps my learned friend could clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What you are doing at the moment as I discern it is attempting to correct the evidence that was given in both situations. You're not suggesting that what is recorded is different from what was actually said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was not sure, Your Honour. That's why perhaps I wanted to bring to Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't notice either of these as not being what was put in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could always have this corrected in cross-examination, perhaps, unless my learned friend wants to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Negodic, at Babin Kuk, at the entrance, was there a mobile anti-aircraft gun with three barrels, 20 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Mobile, three-barrelled gun? I've already said during the previous examination that in my opinion that would be in the area of Orsan, but that is the area towards Babin Kuk. I mean, that's what I mean. I don't know whether 100 metres here or there makes a difference as far as you're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the stationary, three-barrel, 20-millimetre cannon, was it by the Neptune Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I think, as far as I know. I mean, I only know about the three-barrelled gun that I talked about just now. Perhaps it was marked on some maps before, and then perhaps it was placed on a vehicle later. But whether that actually happened or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the commanders of the anti-aircraft defence, were they Vuletic, Kraljevic, Jejina, and others?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show the witness D35 and D36, please. Defence Exhibits D35 and D36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there is a confusion in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 35 and 36. These two pictures that the usher has are fine. I think that that is 35 and 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, tell me, what do you see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: This could be the three-barrel gun, yes. But sir, I don't know what this means, in town, "U Gradu."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the caption. I'm interested in hearing what you have to say as an artillery man in terms of what is here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be a three-barrel gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it a 20-millimetre anti-aircraft gun, the three-barrelled one?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it can be used as an anti-aircraft weapon. But it can also be used as an anti-personnel gun. But I see that you keep putting these questions to me as an expert person, but I already told you that it was my VES. I know perhaps 5 per cent more than you do about these things, but our knowledge about this is more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear. Please don't mind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Of course this is not an examination, but I'm just asking about what you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We had an interlude then when it was impossible for the interpreters to follow because you were both speaking at once. If you could remember that. And could I note that there seems to be a technical problem because what is displayed on the screens is hardly recognisable at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do apologise for speaking so fast. And you are right, the light seems to be wrong, and the barrels cannot be seen. But I think that on the photograph itself, the witness can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it can be seen, the second barrel can be seen. And then I may infer that it is what we said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the second photograph now. Do you know what is on this picture? Are you familiar with it? It is the cab of a truck. Have you ever seen this in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this. Kobra it says in the front. And people told jokes about the man who was the driver. But I don't know anything else that I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it is not being contested that -- we don't need the pictures any longer, Mr. Usher. Thank you. So mobile cannon, it was positioned on a truck as can be seen on these photographs, and it was not linked to a particular position in the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is also correct that as for operations and as for the deployment of these anti-aircraft guns, mobile and stationary ones, at that time this was decided upon by the commanders of the anti-aircraft defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Of course that's right, but with the approval of General Marinovic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few minutes ago, when I asked you about an HOS unit, you say that you knew that they were only at Srdj, a certain number of HOS members. But did you perhaps hear that HOS units came from Split, Omis [phoen], Markarska, Imotski, and other places?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know anything about that. I don't even know where this group, these ten-odd men came from. I never saw them either. I just know that people talked about it, that they were up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection, Your Honour. Previously, the witness recognised the picture that was a truck, but however my learned friend went on to say from there that "it is not being contested that mobile cannon... It was positioned on a truck as can be seen on these photographs, and it was not linked to a particular position in the town of Dubrovnik." That's not what the witness said. The witness identified the truck and said that people used to make jokes about the driver. There was no issue about a cannon being placed on the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, let's clarify this. On the photograph that you saw, is the anti-aircraft gun on the truck?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I said that I think that it is a three-barrelled gun on the truck, the one that was an Orsan. As for other vehicles and other weapons, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: This is the area of Lapad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right, but it doesn't matter now, and it's not in relation to this photograph. While you were in Dubrovnik on the 1st of October 1991 until the 31st of October 1991, did you ever see a three-barrelled gun mounted on a truck?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Considering that you were chief of artillery in the command of the defence of Dubrovnik, considering that you had your own purview, you had under you personnel and equipment that you were supposed to take care of, were you informed in detail and were you aware of all that was going on during combat operations from Dubrovnik? Meaning when Croatian forces were opening fire against JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as my artillery was concerned, I know what assignments they had been given and what they are supposed to shoot at. As far as other units are concerned, I had no time to take an interest in the orders they were given and their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did it ever happen that the orders given concerning combat operations were not obeyed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It never happened as far as the artillery's concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how about the other units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I cannot give you any answer to that because I do not know enough to be able to discuss this subject at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that discipline among artillery troops under you was very high?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I could not quite call it discipline. However, since I was with them at all times, they did respect and obey my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Responding to a question from the Trial Chamber, you said that the Croatian Army on the 6th of December numbered between 400 to 450 troops, not counting the police.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I said that this number, 450, could correspond to reality as far as I know. There could have been some more or slightly less. But that's my assumption of their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, reading from Exhibit P160, and that is the map which has a typewritten diagram of organisational and establishment scheme of the Dubrovnik sector, it says "58 commanders and commanding officers, 22 NCOs, 1.060 soldiers, a total of 1.149 on the 3rd of December"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this really. I would say if you had asked me based on this document that it was around 1100. However, you mentioned the detachment of armed vessels, and if we counted that maybe we could arrive at your number. But not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because this was approved by the command of the Dubrovnik defence and the commander, Nojko Marinovic, I suppose. They had exact numbers of their troops as of the 3rd of December, as written here, and that number is 1.149 total. And I'm asking you this because the difference between that number and the one you gave us is great.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I told you it was only my opinion. However, while we are dealing with this map, sir, it doesn't matter at all how you got hold of that map and who gave it to you. But I've already stated that my firing positions are not precisely indicated on that map dated 3rd December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if my learned friend is going to continue questioning the witness on those numbers, perhaps the witness can be given the map to examine and respond appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that would be sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, may we have map P160 to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Negodic, we were talking about the right top corner of the map, indicating the organisational and establishment structure of the Dubrovnik sector, including commands and all the military units included in the defence of Dubrovnik. Do you see below that the total number, officers 58; NCOs, 22; soldiers, 1.069. Do you see the total number, 1.149?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you see in the right-hand top corner it says "as of 3rd December 1991"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. But I'm telling you again that this deployment of artillery is not the reality -- does not correspond to the reality as it was on the 3rd of December 1991. That's only --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But please, would you comment on the numbers.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I told you before that when I indicated certain numbers, it was only my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But tell me, when you are saying that the positions indicated on the map do not reflect the reality.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I mean that this is not the deployment as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you provide this map to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Certainly not. I have no idea how these maps ended up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you used to see a map like this in the headquarters of the Dubrovnik command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. Certainly not with this legend, because it must have been used at the level of commanders of the town defence. Certainly not at the level of unit commander. Unit commanders would only have been able to indicate numbers of their own troops and deployment of their own equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you say the same about that other map indicating thrusts of action with those little squares?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, the deployment in that case also does not reflect the reality in the period around the 6th of December, the one that the lady wanted me to put little arrows on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you don't know the origins of that map?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who could have provided them and who could have brought them here, if you understand what I mean. If you allow me to add one more thing, in my opinion these maps could only have come from a military archive. Now, who would have had the license to take them out and provide them and bring them here is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Concerning that period when you were chief of artillery, did you draw the deployment of your troops and the position of your weapons regularly on your own maps in that period, October, November, December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: You're asking me about the drawing of the maps. That was left to operative workers. And I used maps to show the troops' different locations and targets, and when I was talking to the commander of the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I understand what you said about operative workers and the drawing of the maps. But I would like to know strictly in the professional sense: When operative workers drew some maps that concerned strictly the artillery, did you keep such maps as chief of artillery?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. I had maps in front of me in the place where I was sitting indicating combat positions and the target sectors, and that was the map intended for the chief of artillery. Similar maps were given to the head of engineering and the commander of anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that period, October, November, December, you had such maps with you indicating the positions of artillery pieces you had under your command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but the real attack against Dubrovnik had not started at that time. Those maps dealt with the area of Konavle in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But was an overview of combat positions done also for the subsequent months, November, December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you and myself that we have to pay attention and make pauses between questions and answers because of interpreters. I will do my best on my part. Can you tell me, until what time did you stay in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Until the beginning of 1996, end January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, in August 1991, you joined with the rank of reserve captain first class?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Correct. That is the rank when I joined in middle of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And by 1996, you only earned the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a bit unusual since you were chief of artillery, after all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It is a bit unusual to you and even to my compatriots, not less Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I got retired as a civilian. I don't know if this is a satisfactory answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said: "Civilian disability pension."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And now, you are registered as a retired major in reserve. Is that the way it's regulated?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. Only a month after I was pensioned off and received civilian disability pension, I was erased from the records as reserve officer at the disposal of the Croatian state, and I am now in archives, which means that I have no liability towards the military department.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were not a professional military man?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mate Sarlija, also known as Daidza, was he superior to Nojko Marinovic in the military hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that they were on the same level with the proviso that Mate Daidza Sarlija covered the area from Metkovici towards Stane, and I don't know which area was covered by the other person. I don't know what rank he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Before you came to testify here, did you have opportunity to see any JNA maps entered into evidence indicating JNA positions and positions of the Croatian Army in October-December 1991? Did anyone show you such maps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: What do you mean? Do you mean the maps we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, similar maps, but belonging to the other side, JNA.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you maybe aware of the report of the artillery expert Jusuf Voje [phoen] concerning artillery activities in Dubrovnik in November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That name tells me nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did your mortars fire always from the same positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: There was only one day when two mortars were placed on one firing position and returned again on the same day to their original position. I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify, what was this all about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That happened in the first half of November. The target was the territory between Zarkovica and Bosanka, fired from the Bogosica Park firing position. Later, orders were given to them to return to the original firing position which was the SDK building. As far as all the rest is concerned, all the other firing positions were fixed positions, apart from the position of Maljutka, which had a basic and a backup position. And the same goes for the recoilless cannon. But all the other guns had fixed positions because we could not allow our troops to be killed needlessly because we had both natural and manmade protections. We had small reinforced concrete booths and gun enplacements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, can you tell me whether you know what wandering mortars are?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: We never used that expression, and I wouldn't be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during the firing, did you change the positions of mortars?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, once in the first half of November, from the combat position of -- I mean, there are two or three names. It's Dubrovkinja or SDK. On the combat positions between Zarkovica and Bosanka, these two mortars were returned to their basic combat position. That's the only thing I know. As for mortars, they were only at their stationary, fixed positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So in the period of October, November, and December, it was only once that the position of the mortar was changed; namely, when from the position of the SDK of Dubrovkinja, two mortars were transferred to Bogosica Park and immediately after that they were returned to the initial position at the SDK. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that you did not know the exact day, the exact date, but that that was the only relocation that took place between the 8th and 13th of November 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness Defence Exhibit D28 and D37.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, can you recognise the area, the weapon, or perhaps even the person in this picture?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I recognise the person, and it may be that combat position, too. You heard my answer a few minutes ago. I said in the first half of the month of November, but I think that it was between the 8th and the 13th. So you should take that into account, that I think it was between the 8th and the 13th. But I see that you have the 4th written over here. I did not say that it was certainly between the 8th and the 13th. Are you following me? But I did say that it was in the first half of November. I think that this is that combat position. And the man is Zoran Primic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I heard you, and it is correct that you said in the first half of the month of November that the mortar moved to Bogosica Park. But in response to my learned friend's question you said that this only relocation took place in the period between the 8th and 13th of November, but you did not know exactly which day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I do not know exactly which day, but I assume it was between the 8th and the 13th when there was quite a bit of firing at Dubrovnik. And that's how I said that it was between the 8th and the 13th and now it turned out to be the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Even if you did not see this picture --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning. The witness is being shown two photographs which bear the date 4/11, and the year is not even clearly indicated here. Of course, they have been tendered as Defence exhibits. I do not know whether they have been marked for identification or through which witnesses. I do not think that it's fair by this witness to ask to respond to -- on these photographs in this manner, with regard to the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think there is substance in that objection, Ms. Mahindaratne. But I think what is important for both Mr. Negodic is for Mr. Rodic is to realise that there is no evidence at the moment that the date 4 November, whatever year, is correct. So that may be a correct date; it may not be a correct date, Mr. Negodic. We do not know. That just happens to be the date on this document which the Defence has put before us. So don't assume it is correct. It may be correct. We don't know. I think that is the position at the moment, is it not, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would just like to point out that although these are Defence exhibits, these photographs, but these photographs were only taken from the film that the Prosecution introduced as P66. And the film shows what happened in Dubrovnik in October, November, December 1991. I shall go on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position, though, that we have no verification of the date depicted here of 4 November as being correct at the present time. What you just observed is why I suggested that the submission put against you was not well founded. That was the first thing I said when Ms. Mahindaratne objected. I then went on, though, to point out that at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the moment we have nothing to verify this particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I shall go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, the man in the photograph in Bogosica Park, you said that it was Zoran Primic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you know whether there was any firing from this position in Bogosica Park in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Zoran Primic is in civilian clothes, I gather, in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the rest? Most of the members of the artillery, were they dressed in the same way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, in that period. Maybe you did notice that he has a Motorola radio transmitter on his left hip.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what about the other months, apart from November 1991? Was there any firing from the position in Bogosica Park?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir. I've already said that, that it was only once that any firing took place from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, did you give a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 12th and 13th of December 2003? The investigators being Richard Philips and Azim Arshad?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know their names, but that should be the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you told me what you knew about these events and when you told them, did you read this and then check it out and sign it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it was read out to me. But it was told to me -- or rather, I was told that some corrections could be made. And even if there are still mistakes in the text, when I come here, that I could correct some of the mistakes that were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read paragraph 22 from your statement where it says "there was insufficient space to form a battery, which would also be at risk to counterbattery fire. We could not afford to lose a lot of troops in one attack." Do you remember that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, roughly, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I read it out exactly, word for word.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: You read it well. But this type of statement that I was making refers to the period before the engineering people started building the reinforced concrete huts. If we're talking about a park that is not a natural shelter, then that would mean sacrificing one's personnel. That is why two mortars were placed by the SDK building, because it is a concrete building. Next door to it is an old stone building where ammunition was kept. The wall is about 70 centimetres thick, and that's where it was kept. And they sought shelter in the atomic shelter when there was no firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, when did -- the engineering people started building shelters for your artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date. But it could be approximately the beginning of the month of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you fired shells from your mortars, did you expect return fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: All indicators seemed to show that return fire was to be expected. However, these sheltered positions, mortar positions that we just discussed, were covered from view, from all sides. You could control the flying and the landing of the shell. There was an JNA observation post at Zarkovica. When we fired a gun, they could see us as well as we could see them. And in the entire period, October, November, it never happened that the shell -- that a shell fell in the perimeter of 500 metres from us. An observer could very easily control the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm now interested in the mortar.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Its firing position was in the old arsenal, in the old barracks which was taken over later by the trade enterprise Dubrovkinja. They built the SDK building. And in that space between buildings, mortars were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that this position from the SDK building, the mortar position was so sheltered that the JNA could not see it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So even when it was firing, they were unable to locate its position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are the pine trees very tall in Bogosica Park?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but they are few and far between. They are not densely planted, as you can see on the picture. You cannot have a multitude of targets because the positioning of the pine trees hinders targeting -- hinders multiple targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would that mean that the pine trees interfere with the trajectory of the missiles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. The crown of the trees is in the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the other mortar positions in Dubrovnik in the period of October, November, and December 1991. Were they also fixed, not subject to change?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, all the rest were fixed positions. This unit that you see in the picture, this man, Primic, was commander of that unit. The unit was divided into two parts. One was placed near the SDK building, and the other east of the Old Town in the park. That position was called Lazaret. That area is sheltered by natural features, and it is very difficult to hit it. It is not visible from the sea, from boats and ships, and it is also invisible from Zarkovica, although it is relatively close.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if I understood you correctly, the mortars to the east in Lazaret are also sheltered so the JNA cannot see them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The Isle of Lokrum is in their way. That isle is in front of Lazaret and Ploca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During that period, October to December 1991, was there a popular term, "Charlie," in Dubrovnik, current in Dubrovnik for a gun placed on top of a truck?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that. I may not be a professional soldier or an expert, but I cannot fathom a mortar being placed on a truck. It would be lethal for the crew, for the person who was filling the shells, feeding the shells into the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say it's dangerous, you probably mean that it's placed on a hard surface?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to adjust that surface to the needs of the mortar by placing some sandbags?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Let us suppose that you put sandbags and you fire one shell. With even a minor shift and the move of the barrel, the explosive effect would be great and you would not be able to fire again from the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. I've already asked you this. There's just one more thing concerning the situation with mortars. I'll read out to you starting with paragraph 20 of your statement, what you said. "Until the 6th of December 1991, we had two mortars at Bogosica Park in Pile. These were then" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not "until the 6th of December 1991," but it says "before 6th December 1991 we had two mortars at Bogosica Park in Pile." And it gives a different meaning when you say "until the 6th of December 1991."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may or may not be a difference in meaning; it's unclear. But the distinction is there. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It says that before or until this date you had two mortars at Bogosica Park in Pile. These were then moved to another position near Dubrovkinja company. These weapons were manned by Primic and Pilas.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know how this statement could have been worded in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this way. When you now read this, Bogosica Park, you said in the next breath in Pile. I cannot be wrong about this because I lived in Dubrovnik for 50 years. And I know very well that Bogosica Park is six to seven hundred metres away from Pile. How could I have stated a thing like this? How could I have said that it was in Pile if it's 700 metres as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about this distance? 600 to 600 [as interpreted] metres as the distance between Bogosica Park and Pile?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Approximately 600 metres, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say this, what could be the other two mortars that could have been moved from the Dubrovkinja building or the SDK? Would they be the mortars that had been placed in Bogosica Park at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The firing position near the SDK building and the Lazaret Park belonged to the same unit. Those two mortars that fired in the beginning of November are the same two mortars whose basic firing position was at the SDK building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you say that this is a mistake to say that the location was in Pile, let us disregard that. What are the two mortars, or rather what is the position of the two mortars that were moved around the 6th of December to a position near Dubrovkinja company? Were these mortars from the Lazaret position or from the Bogosica Park?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Since so many questions seem to revolve around Bogosica Park, maybe that answer was worded in such a way that it is still clear to me what I meant, but you may view it differently from your perspective. I'm repeating again: Bogosica Park is a firing position that was used only once. How it was translated, I don't know. Maybe it lends itself to various interpretations. But I'm telling you that fire was opened only once from Bogosica Park. All the rest of the time these mortars were near the Dubrovkinja building or the SDK position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another objection that is with regard to counsel's question. My learned friend has interpreted paragraph 20 of the statement and goes on to say "what are the two mortars or rather what is the position of the two mortars that were moved around the 6th of December to the position of Dubrovkinja company?" No, there was no reference at all that the position was moved around the 6th. In the statement, it says before the 6th of December, there was a position in Bogosica Park.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no quarrel with the situation because I read the statement. It's not an issue whether it was before or on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The only thing that is in issue is do you mean that these mortars were shifted from Bogosica Park only once, on that day when they were fired from? Did you mean to say that they were then moved to the SDK building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That's what I said. They were taken from the firing position near the SDK, brought to the Bogosica Park, and then returned to their basic firing position, that is, the building next to the SDK. Those are two and the same mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that those mortars were under the command of Zoran Primic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Zoran Primic report this to you in the same way regarding the shifting of the position of these two mortars?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I asked him, because I was not aware of the goings-on on that day. We called him on his Motorola, and he said he felt it was necessary -- because he was at the Srdj hill, he felt it was necessary to fire at a target behind. I told him to do that.
