But then return to his original position. He may have given some clarification later, but you will forgive me if I don't remember it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were only informed by Zoran Primic that he had returned these mortars?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him for a report, how much ammunition was spent, and how much was left at the firing position because we couldn't afford to spend so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The lack or the shortage of ammunition was constant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the same is true of cannons? They were not shifted from their positions in the period October through December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Speaking of firing positions that we placed under the bridge like this ZIS cannon, it's main purpose was to face the Srdj fortress and Zarkovica. And there was no need to move towards another direction which would be less efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, during firing missions, do you have a visual overview of all the artillery pieces under your command, all the pieces that you're in charge of as chief of artillery?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, from that firing position on the -- from that position I was on, on the 6th of December, I cannot see my own firing position. However, when orders are given to fire a, let's say, 120-millimetre shell I can see from my firing position the landing of that shell. Whether it is left of the Srdj hill, whether it hit the Srdj hill, or whether it hit on the right so that I'm able to correct it. But from my firing post overlooking the cannon itself, I cannot see the other firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean the other combat positions of your weapons, your artillery pieces are not visible?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you're following the action of your own artillery, if you're looking at JNA positions to see where your shells from your side are landing, based on what you see from observing the fire, are you able to discern the exact location of your artillery pieces? Can you tell where they're firing from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: When a 120-millimetre shell is fired from the area of auto kamp in Lapad, no fire was opened from the 82-millimetre position which we called the ex-barracks. For instance, when I give orders for this shell to be fired, I can follow it. It targeted mainly a position around the Srdj hill, and I can see it with the naked eye, without binoculars, I can see where it lands. Because we are targeting an area; we are not targeting a specific, fixed object. It doesn't really matter exactly where it fell, 50 metres into the depth or 50 metres forward. What matters is that it hits the area around the Srdj fortress.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's not quite what I asked. During firing missions, do you have a visual overview of your own artillery pieces? And I further asked, from observing the fire of your own artillery and from looking where the shells land, near JNA positions, can you tell that the position of your own artillery pieces had not moved, either by 50 or 100 metres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I can say that the question is not really very clear. However, a commander at a firing or combat position knows my location, where I am as an observer, one who is going to guide his fire. When I say 200 to the right, it doesn't mean that it's his 200 to the right. That is why he has someone who is doing the calculation for him, or rather who is going to plot on the map what my order meant. 200 to the right, it is further from him. Do you understand what I'm saying? And it is not necessary for us to have visual contact, the observer and the combat position, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Everything I asked you in relation to visual contact is precisely with a view to seeing whether you could see during the actual operations whether one of your weapons moved from one combat position to another. That was the point; that was what I was driving at.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I've already answered, that there is no reason whatsoever for us to move anything, say, on the 6th of December. For example, a well-fortified position of an individual mortar, and the ammunition that was placed in huts, why would we drag all of that elsewhere? And we would not have gained anything. We are not firing at full range. If we have 120-millimetre weapons, half of the range is good enough for us, for our objectives. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You say that you say no reason, but that is your assumption. Now, I'm asking you, what if the JNA had located the position of your weapons and if they are counterfiring now. Would your people stay in the same position or would they move their weapon elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In the best case, they would move into the shelter, the concrete shelter, the huts. However, I have already stated several times, and I claim that from the JNA combat positions, objectives were not targeted by way of artillery. It is only an area that was targeted. It wasn't one army fight the against another. If it were the way you're putting your questions, sir, I've already told you an observer from Zarkovica sees the cannon position of the cannon that is targeting him just as he is directly targeting the position of Zarkovica. The point -- if the point was to target that particular position of the Croatian Army, it would not have been difficult for him to find it. He would have found it very easily, that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And if a JNA observer would easily find that combat position of yours, would you still stay there, or would you move?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In such a small area, sir, we have only that one good shelter. We do not have any other place where we could move that weapon. The only thing that would be "ideal" is that particular position. There is not another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. If I have understood what you have been saying, and correct me if I'm wrong, the crews of your mortars and other weapons that were firing at JNA positions were protected from superior artillery fire of the JNA by virtue of the fact that they were in the well-selected, well-fortified positions in Dubrovnik. Is that right? Is that the right answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Almost in all positions, except Babin Kuk, mortars and the Maljutka on the very coastline. The Maljutka has poor natural shelter. And the mortars in the area of the former auto kamp were among the olive trees and pine trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about these mortars from Babin Kuk, were they moved from there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, because that is where their combat position was made, because reinforced concrete huts were placed there. And then big slabs of stone were brought and placed in front of the huts. So a shell that would hit that area would be activated on the stone rather than on the reinforced concrete hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and on the 6th of December did you have any artillery pieces in the area of Sustjepan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That's where the infantry part of the 2nd Battalion was. Now, except for a hand-held launcher, whether they had something else, that's something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the 1st Battalion, did it have any mortars within its establishment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is only the artillery that had mortars. The 82-millimetre mortar otherwise would not belong to the establishment of the artillery. It is actually a weapon that accompanies the infantry, but the situation was such that it was included in the artillery just like recoilless guns were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. So we agree that the artillery forces of the JNA far outnumbered the artillery forces and their weapons of the Croatian side in the period from October to December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for the tactics of the Croatian forces, precisely because there were so few artillery weapons, was the impression being created that there were more weapons than there actually were by relocating the existing weapons from one position to another?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Not as far as the artillery was concerned. But I assume that in the anti-aircraft defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Particularly because these were mounted on vehicles, so yes, it is very likely that that would be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it correct that 30 per cent of your artillery pieces and mortars did not have any sighting equipment and were not fully effective?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The artillery pieces were in proper condition, but there weren't enough sights available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for sighting equipment when you were in a position to do so, of course, depending on the operations, did you take them off and take them from one position to another?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of translation you have there, but I think that I said in my statement that once positions were taken in terms of one mortar, that then the sighting equipment would be taken and then it would be moved to another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read paragraph 21 from your statement out to you. You said: "Some weapons did not have sighting equipment."

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: "So we had sometimes to remove sighting equipment and move it from one position to another."

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: This can be understood in two different ways. If I have a unit, for example, like the mortars that we refer to just now in the area of the auto kamp, I don't know how people are going to understand what I'm saying. But from the position of one mortar, when we go to another position of another mortar, then perhaps that could be a different firing position of the entire unit. I don't know whether you're following me. But I meant these firing positions, from one mortar position to another. It can be 15 metres, but it can be understood that it's a firing position on the completely opposite side of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did you have these sights on every firing position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but not enough of them. For example, if there are four mortars and only two pieces of sighting equipment, then we would have to shift them from one to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, when you moved sights from one weapon to another, did you rectify them as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The rectification had taken place before that, at least that's what the report said, that the rectification of sighting equipment had taken place and that all the weapons were ready. I did not have time to check that. It was left to the commanders of the units involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my next question. Did you have time and opportunity to do that kind of thing, to check this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have a trained man on every crew who could actually perform the rectification needed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Almost every commander of every unit had completed reserve officers' school for artillery officers, except for Primic. As far as I know, he held no rank in the army, but he -- his conduct was impeccable. We did not have an appropriate replacement, so we just provided a person from the land survey department. And it was very easy for him to master things that another layman would have taken six months to master.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you could not in terms of space and time check this out yourself personally - that is to say, the rectification, whether it was performed or not - are you sure then that you had appropriate precision from your weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, sir, this cannot be stated with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what about the direction and elevation of the weapons? And I'm referring to mortars. How did you ascertain that when you did not have the right kind of sighting equipment? And the same goes for cannons because we see that not all cannons had sighting equipment either.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I've already said that with one piece of sighting equipment we would work on one target and calculate it. And then we would use the same sight and put it onto another piece of equipment. That's what I already said. I cannot give any other explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the elevation? Was it calculated by using a quadrant? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I had sufficient trust in the people who had completed reserve officers' schools for these weapons, and there's no need to go in and check on them whether the quality was at proper level. And there wasn't really very much time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me then that one cannot say that there wasn't any misfiring because there was not enough equipment and not all the weapons were in order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, in the army in the time of the former Yugoslavia and hundreds and hundreds of times after that, at meetings and at exercises, even when there were full preparations that had been carried out, there were nevertheless such situations, let alone with this degree of preparation. Even if weapons are brand new, this kind of thing can happen. It would be a lie if I were to say the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the ammunition that you used, where was it manufactured, especially the ammunition used for mortars?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I cannot really answer that question. It came from TO storage. As far as I know, we got it from Ploca, Metkovici. As far as I can remember, it was in the warehouses in the reserves of the Territorial Defence headquarters and in their respective areas they had this and probably came from there, and perhaps even from Split. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you use mortar shells that were Croatian-made?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I'm not really in a position to answer your question. This question was not one that was ever raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But I'm just wondering whether you knew whether there were any Croatian-made mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember that. But I do know that Croatia does manufacture mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have proper tables for all ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. However for the ZIS cannon, from two firing positions, we did not have sighting equipment. So it would not have worked out that way. We could not have firing tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as far as Croatian-made mortar shells are concerned, did you have appropriate firing tables?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I'm not sure about the shells. But if there were such shells, then they would have been accompanied by appropriate tables because it makes no sense to fire one kind of shell and not to have those tables, but tables for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps what the precision was of the Croatian-made shells?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that. I mean, I don't know whether they were there, so then how can I speak of their precision. One has to do with the other, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what targets did you fire at the most on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: From what firing positions, tell me specifically, or are you asking me overall?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what targets did you take on most frequently.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Srdj and Zarkovica. When I say "Srdj," I mean the fortress of Srdj and the slopes of the Srdj hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I moved to another subject before I asked you a question that was supposed to come before. In that period, October through December 1991, did something unusual happen such as a weapon failing to fire because a barrel exploded or the missile got stuck?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I never received a report to that effect. There were later some stories that some shells, in maybe two or three cases, were not actually fired -- failed to fired. But I don't know whether it was the ignition that failed or something else. I don't know the specific reason for these failures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who directed the fire from your artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, do you mean who guided the artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Answer this first.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, I was at a firing position above the artillery piece that was located under the bridge. And from that position, I could see both the Srdj hill and that other place which was called Vidikovac, Zarkovica. So that I was able at close range to tell the man manning the cannon directly what to target. In another case, there was a cannon which only once hit the area around Pobrezje and did not fire any more. I asked them to fire 120-millimetre shell for me to see where it would land, and I would be able to correct the fire. And in another case, I wanted them to fire to the right of the Srdj hill where the ski lift emerges. There was an overshoot after the first fire, and I was quite all right with that as long as it did not land too close. Since that weapon fired an overshoot, it covered the area of an infantry attack from the side of Bosanka village towards the Srdj hill, and that was all right as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, are you saying that on the 6th of December, you were the one calculating the elements of fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So who was doing that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The person at the firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who did the correction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: When the first shell was fired, I would see with the naked eye where the shell fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Does that mean that you were in contact with all your artillery crews?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That was physically impossible. One person could not direct fire from three firing positions. The rocket's laser was given the task to fire at a specific target and there was no need to test it anymore. As far as mortars were concerned, the one at the SDK building was given the task to shoot at the right side of the SDK towards the Srdj hill. And looking at that shot, I thought that there was no more need for me to be in constant contact with them. The same is true of the mortar in the area of auto kamp Lapad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did somebody on the crew of those mortars direct the fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: They fired at this area with brief breaks, and then in Lapad they took over because it was physically impossible to sustain. I absented myself when I was going, as I said, to drive those wounded persons. So the command took it upon themselves for the communication between the Srdj fortress and the command on the one hand and the command and the firing position on the other hand to be sustained. So that people near Srdj were directing fire through the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Nojko Marinovic was up to snuff and following the situation both in terms of the weapons available and the positions in the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just add for the picture to be clearer: You already mentioned that at the beginning you wanted me to confirm certain names of people who were on the command of the defence of the town. You said that one of them, Marinkovic was the head of the defence. I don't know that. But I know that he was a professional officer in the artillery so that in the command we did have a person who was professionally trained for this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You don't mean Nojko Marinovic, you mean another officer from the headquarters of the command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe they did this job together. But since he was better qualified, then Nojko Marinovic, who was as far as I know an infantry man, although even as an infantry man he might have been familiar enough with 82-millimetre mortars because they accompany the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this man then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Mirko Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know specifically on the 6th of December 1991 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who was in command of anti-aircraft guns, the three-barrel gun and the single-barrel gun placed on top of trucks that were moving around the town and opening fire from various positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Do you mean commanders who were manning these weapons? Or do you mean who was in charge of the entire air defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I mean the commanders manning these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question has been asked as to whether the witness knows who was in command of anti-aircraft guns, the three-barrel gun, and the single-barrel gun placed on top of trucks that were moving around the town and opening fire from various positions. That was not the evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is my question. And I'm asking it based on the previous answers I got from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, your question is not only asking answers about one matter or some matters, but it's assuming others to be correct that have not been established. It's not established that trucks were moving around the town and opening fire from various positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, the mobile weapons that we discussed such as anti-aircraft guns, were they placed on top of trucks? Were they stationary or were they moving around the town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, as I stated before, as far as I know, the third-barrel gun, and I spoke about one weapons, not weapons, I said that as far as I know, there was a three-barrel gun placed on top of a vehicle. And I suppose that it was moving around because it did not have an actual target. It is the kind of weapon that has to come out into a clearing in order to be able to fire. Whether they wandered about town or not I really am not able to tell you in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in command of that weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Are you finished? Can I answer? You already mentioned it. I believe that the one on the three-barrel gun was Jejina, or maybe Vuletic. You mentioned them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were there any anti-aircraft weapons located inside houses and opening fire, targeting Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: You mean an anti-aircraft weapon placed inside a house and opening fire? This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there any fire of this kind from the tower of St. Ivan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, from all I know, and I've stated this a number of times in response to your questions and those of the Prosecutor, on the fortresses and inside the town, there were no anti-aircraft or artillery weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this again: On the tower of St. Luka, was there a gun, 52 millimetres, single barrel? Tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, along the ramparts of the Old Town, close to the walls, near the Pile gates, were there 82-millimetre mortars opening fire from this location and using the walls as a cover, as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the period October through December 1991, did mortars ever open fire from these positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: There were never any firing position from mortars in that place. The nearest position in the Old Town is the position I mentioned before, and that is the Lazaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen in the southern tower near the bell that a mortar was placed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the southern tower, was there an artillery position?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is a mistake by the interpreter. The previous answer of the witness was no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you picked that up, Mr. Rodic? There has been a correction in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer at 57:19 is "yes." The interpreter tells us that is a mistake, and the answer given was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From the area of the fish shop in the Old Town, was there an anti-aircraft machine-gun active, 7.7 -- 12.7 millimetres calibre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there a truck carrying mortar active along the JNA street up to Oburtska [phoen] Street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that from the first of October to the 31st October 1991, you were only once in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said it was on the 6th of December 1991 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, how, based on what do you claim that there were no artillery weapons or fire opened from the Old Town or in the vicinity? Based on what information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, every commander or chief was responsible for his troops. And I was with them every day. And I suppose I know enough about their movements. I did not go down into the town because if I had gone, then the troops would have followed me. I suppose I know best where my artillery weapons are, at which firing position, what they're targeting, and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please look again at the top right-hand corner of that map, this organisational and establishment diagram of the structure of the defence of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you go from the first little block down the whole way, do you see a little block where it says "MAV 76 and 82" when you follow the line in the middle?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that is supposed to mean, this acronym, MAV, M-A-V, 76 and 82?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I would very much like to help you, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this abbreviation or acronym means in the little hut, in the little block below, says "DST 82, V-3"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I believe that is a recoilless cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you look to left of these little blocks, these -- do you see the scheme of the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you see, for instance, in the fourth and the fifth little blocks from the top in the scheme of the 1st Battalion, mortars 120 and 82 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. That's why I asked you. Sir, who could have given you this? Because as the map does not reflect the reality, neither does this diagram because there was no infantry battalion that had an 82-millimetre gun, whereas I, in my artillery unit, was short of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that there were mortars under the command of the 1st Battalion, according to this scheme, this diagram?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, if you believe this scheme you would have to believe that they had 120-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the composition of the 1st Battalion, is it true, then, that according to this diagram within your competence you would have detachment -- these recoilless cannons, this last little block, 76 and 82 millimetres, and the Maljutka, and you have on the upper left-hand side next to the first box, next to the command, you have 128. And I think that is a single-barrel rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So would this then be -- would these then be the weapons under your competence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The rocket launcher and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to this diagram.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the diagram, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about these cannons and the Maljutka and the rocket launcher, would they belong to you according to this diagram?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how the diagram was made up, and the rocket launchers come under the 1st Battalion. That's where they're -- it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the middle, please, the central part of what we have stuck to the map here. And on the left it says "authorised by Colonel Mirko Katanic," and he is precisely the officer you said was a professional and well versed in the artillery?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In the left-hand corner in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you something else. When during the examination-in-chief on the 22nd of April you responded to the questions from my learned colleague, you explained the positions of the artillery pieces, the weapons to the north on the ramparts of the Old Town, you see it here. It's marked here. You said that you weren't quite sure whether on the 6th of December there was the Strijela weapon there or not, or whether it was the Igla type anti-aircraft weapon. Take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, I will take a look at that, but I do know what location I'm talking about. But I have to put myself right. You said on the ramparts, on the walls, the northern walls of the Old Town, right? That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I just said the marking was there. That's where it was marked.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Then be more precise. It is to the north of the walls of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I said that it said north?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Gentlemen, you're running an ongoing conversation, the two of you together. No interpreter could possibly cope with that. Is it time, Mr. Rodic, to have a break while you settle down again?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have a break then, Mr. Negodic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, before the break, we were looking at the location on the map linked to the symbol denoted as -- denoted on the northern side of the Old Town. Do you see that mark there, the symbol?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I have to put you right again. Your expression "on the north side of the Old Town," that would make it that it was on the north side on the Old Town, the weapon, whereas I'm saying that the weapon was to the north of the Old Town, 200 metres away, 100 metre -- 50 is -- 200 metres away. So Mr. Rodic, that's not one and the same thing. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you completely. And I'm not insisting on anything. We'll get through the explanation slowly.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I take advantage of this occasion to ask you that a correction be made. I don't know when I would have the right to speak up and say what I have to say. So with the Court's indulgence, may I do that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen from the Defence, a little patience, if you will. After my testimony on Friday, I thought through what I had said, and I came -- I realised that I gave a statement which referred to the 6th of December, that is to say that, in the attack, vessels had also taken part, ships. So in that sense, in order to paint a clearer picture of the situation on the 6th of December, I hereby state the following: That the ships were in territorial waters of the Republic of Croatia in the Bay of Zupa Dubrovacka, but they didn't go into operation and attack the town. For us to understand the situation better, let me give a brief explanation, if I may. We are witnesses to the fact that on Friday, there was some interruption in the working of the apparatuses here, the technology. So my answers also run along those lines. That is to say, I have a computer in my head, and it has been 13 years since the time of the event. So I do hope you'll understand me when I say that my computer went wrong and that men can be used up just like machines can. So I ask for the Court's indulgence and understanding. So if I correct my statement, as I have just done, I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we understand from what you now say, Mr. Negodic, that you want it to stand as your evidence that on the 6th of December 1991, there was no fire from ships of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I would like to follow on from that correction you just made to ask you who jogged your memory and reminded you of that. Who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I went through the matter in my own mind because I had two days, the weekend, to think over what I had said. And I don't wish you, sir, to understand that I am cheering any team here. I'm not in that role of cheerer. So please believe me when I say I don't seek any revenge. I'm not burdened either ethnically speaking or religiously speaking. And I'm just an ordinary man. I would have fought anybody who had attacked Yugoslavia. That's just the way that I'm fighting this case, too. But as I had so many questions from the Prosecution and of course from you yourself, you know what it's like. One puts oneself right. You say something and you remember it might not have been like that exactly as you put it, so you put yourself right. So for a better understanding for us all, I wanted to make that situation clear and clear matters up here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, I was just interested in how come you came by that correction, how you suddenly thought of that, and is that the only thing that you have thought of during the weekend?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I just remembered that there was no talk or stories going round that they had targeted Lapad, Nuncijata, or Pile in the command. Although I had health problems, and I've already told you about them, nobody told me when they came to visit me in hospital, nobody ever mentioned any ships. So then I remembered following that line of thinking that my members didn't mention any attacks launched from the ships. So that's it. Now, what happened before the attack, for example, in November and so on, we have already discussed that. So that's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you happened to remember that you told the Prosecutor that the ships attacked.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether you asked me or the Prosecutor asked me that, I can't quite remember. But what I do remember is that I spoke about the fact that ships had attacked. So I don't want, if I did say that, relating to the 6th of December, then I don't want my statement to be incorrect. That's not my purpose here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you consider that to be very important, did you, when you gave it some thought, whether the ships had attacked that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I took it in sequence. And this brought me to the 6th of December. I don't know whether you understand me. I am a well-brought-up person. I am honest and sincere, and I would be angry if anybody thought that I wasn't telling the truth or wasn't saying something that I'm absolutely certain of. So I think that it would be acceptable, that it is acceptable, that when I put forward my arguments on time, it is well intentioned, and I think that you should accept my correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Negodic, but I am also interested from the other point of view, this targeting of ships on the 6th of December. Now you have denied that. You have denied that they opened fire and that you told us why. You gave us an explanation. But, sir, one essential point of a personal nature, for example, during the examination-in-chief, you didn't stress, you didn't say that you were wounded and injured on that same day, the 6th of December, and that you weren't at your position, taking up your duties for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't important. It wasn't essential. It didn't come up. I suppose the questions were posed in that way that didn't require me to answer that, an answer of that kind. For me to clarify this situation up, I have just explained the situation I was in for you to understand me better. So I assume that the gentlemen, and I've forgotten their names now, that they formulated their questions in such a way that it didn't require me to explain that, to go into that particular explanation. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we come to my learned friend's question of the 6th of December when you said that throughout you were at your combat positions on that particular day; and yet now, today, we have just learnt that you weren't there. And you explained why you were absent, that you were in hospital and so on and so forth. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already given an explanation to Their Honours, to the Trial Chamber, and I gave you an explanation a moment ago yourself when I said that part of the command during my absence was led by Mirko Katanic. And having given you this piece of information, that the man's name was Mirko Katanic, I have also automatically stated that if he was in charge of that part of the business that I wasn't at the combat position on that day. Do you understand me? Are you following me? So it's an indirect answer to you. If I gave you the name of the person doing my work and taking over my duties in the command at that day, he did so because I wasn't there that day by inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, what does it mean when you tell us that Maljutka, the Babin Kuk position, and the crew linked to Maljutka was not able to remain at their positions but had to move due to the effects of the Yugoslav Navy and its ships, its vessels? So where were those vessels shooting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Just as I put myself right and corrected their action, in my mind, I mixed up the dates. The fact that they weren't able to fire because of concentrated fire from a number of ships targeted Lapad and Nuncijata was not on the 6th of December because my corrected statement entails this whole situation around the Maljutka. It is closely linked. It follows on from the other. So if you -- and I have asked you to accept my corrected statement, that on the 6th of December, they did not open fire at the town of Dubrovnik, that is to say, the ships didn't, then automatically it follows that that date is not linked to the Maljutka episode either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I'd like to bring up another point in that connection. Paragraph 30 of your statement, in fact, can he we take a look at that. And you say there: "I was not present, but my men also reported to me that they had been attacked from a naval boat off Lapad, in Lapad Bay. We were told later that night at Dance and also at the Hotel Belvedere during the day there was some shooting from naval weaponry." So that means that in December, you told the investigators this about the fact that the naval vessels had opened fire.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: If I have already stated, sir, that on the 6th of December I got the dates mixed up, just as I have -- just as I explained a moment ago, or rather said that they had put down anchor at the Bay of Zupa, and then we came to the Maljutka situation, so following on from these events, we come to the shooting at Dance and the Hotel Belvedere. Naval vessels returning to the Bay of Kotor would empty out all their ammunition at the Belvedere Hotel, so if this did not happen, it would appear to us to be unusual, an unusual situation that they did not do this. It was just a play on words whether it was the 6th of December or whether it was in the month of November. And let me repeat again, it has been 13 years since then, 13 years have gone by. And I do wish at all costs to actually forget what happened 13 years ago. And now, when the Prosecutor began to question me on this, and you yourself did, too, it is quite natural that a mistake might have slipped in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that nobody spoke to you about or said anything about the fact that the navy on the 6th of December opened fire, whereas in your statement you say later that night I was told about Dance, Belvedere, and so on. So it would appear from that that somebody did tell you something that night on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't have told me that on the 6th of December because if the ships didn't even reach the Dubrovnik territory, but had anchored in the Bay of Zupa, they were ready to go into action but did not go into action. And that's why I said that it was just that night, that I mixed up the two nights, whether it was the 6th of December or, for example, the 6th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 12th of November. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It's not easy, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but maybe just to get back to the text. You read out your statement here, you read through it before you began your testimony here before my learned colleague of the Prosecution started asking you questions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I was given my statement to look through it and correct certain portions. But at that time as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Before the examination-in-chief conducted by my learned colleague, you had a chance to read through --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Complete his response. He has been interrupted halfway through the response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the witness is managing to get pretty good innings in his response. So Mr. Rodic, would you ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Before the examination-in-chief, you read through your statement again, the one you gave to the investigators in December 2003, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. But yes, I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did you read it through, read through it before the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it was given to me so that I could take a look, but quite simply I didn't remark that mistake. I didn't notice the mistake. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, when you read through the statement, did you tell the Prosecutor which points from your statement should be corrected?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did. I think we put right two or three points. But had I remembered, then I would have told them then, and we wouldn't spend this much time on that point, had I remembered to put that point right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. But just tell me, is it true that this paragraph, paragraph 30, after you read this paragraph, you didn't remember to change it before the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Do you believe that paragraph 30 relates to what we're discussing now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to speak in the way you are speaking or the lady from the Prosecution. Unfortunately, I do not have the right to have a piece of paper and a pencil beside me for me to be able to make notes to assist me in solving this problem better. Had I been able to remember everything and had I had time on Thursday and on Friday, I'm sure I would have done it then and wouldn't have waited for the whole weekend to go by. So that's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as long as we're on this subject, I'll read out to you paragraph 18 from your statement. "We had at our disposal the following equipment: Two ZIS cannons, 76 millimetres; five 120-millimetre mortars; seven 82-millimetre mortars; one single-barrel 128-millimetre rocket launcher; two B2 76-millimetre cannons. Some 30 per cent of these weapons did not have sighting devices on them and so they were not functioning fully." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, you received a revised corrected statement that was supposed to be given to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I asked corrections to be made. Two times B1, that is two B1 guns came on the 6th of December. And there were three mortars on that firing position, and you should have these corrections in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, the statement was corrected before you came to testify, but paragraph 18 was not subject to these corrections and it was not signed as such by you. So if we compare this to what you said in your testimony in chief, we have two more mortars of 120 millimetres and two B2 cannons of 76 millimetres. That's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I would like the Prosecutor to explain this because I think you should have been provided with a corrected copy. I signed these three points, and one of them should be that we're not talking about B2 or B1, 76-millimetre cannons; we received them after the 6th of December. And there were not five but three 120-millimetre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to place on the record, the corrections that the witness sought has been provided to the Defence. And there were four corrections made to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These corrections were made. This is not an issue. And the Defence is not saying that it hasn't received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What I am saying, that among these corrections we received, paragraph 18 enumerating the weapons at your disposal had not been changed or modified.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, I can testify that I saw with my own eyes this correction being made, where it was written "two cannons, 76 millimetres." That was crossed out. The number five was crossed out and three was put instead. Why you don't have this, I can't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can my learned friend help us regarding this correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness sought a correction to paragraph 19, and there he wanted us to delete the reference to two B2 76-millimetre cannons which are positioned at 300 metres from St. Michael's church in Lapad. That is the first amendment. And the reference to the two B2 76-millimetre cannons in paragraph 18 is one and the same. That is what the witness is indicating to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the problem, Mr. Rodic, may be that the matter was corrected in one place in the statement, paragraph 19, but not in paragraph 18. But the two paragraphs are dealing with the same types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honour. Then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, let us look at the map now. Please, look at this. The closest symbol for artillery pieces to the area of the Old Town. Tell me, which area, and please look at the map carefully, which area on this diagram is covered by the whole symbol? Does it touch the ramparts and crosses over the ramparts into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I didn't draw this, and I'm not fully qualified to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you to tell us what you see on the map. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Looking at this, one could say that this artillery piece, if you are looking at the road from the town, it should be here. However, when you look at the map, to the right of this artillery piece you will see a red spot where mortar action is designated. 50 metres above the road. Whereas my firing position was right by the sea. What I mean to say is this: I know that this weapon on the upper road was positioned at the starting point of the ski lift, near the platform of the ski lift at a distance of 120 to 150 metres. When I gave you this explanation that it was 50 metres above the road whereas it should be close to the sea, I hope that that should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you simply to answer my question. It's very precise. The symbol of anti-aircraft artillery weapon, can you tell us how is it drawn on the map? Does this symbol cover partly the territory of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, this symbol drawn in near the Old Town was designated by you, was marked by you as an anti-aircraft weapon.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That's what I think it has to be, because there's no other weapon in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to the right of that, the next symbol is a symbol for a mortar.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not drawn in properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We're now only discussing symbols. To the right of the mortar, what does this symbol designate, this little arrow which in the middle has a small arch? What does that designate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: By the location --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Not by the location. I'm asking you what the symbol means.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: You see, on the right side, it has a red little dot. And on the left side, it's connected. I suppose the marking is the same for an anti-aircraft weapon, be it an Igla needle or Strijela arrow. I believe that is the same kind of marking as the one we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance which symbol is used to denote an anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe if it has two little dots on the right side, that should be the anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The symbol for that is like the one on the edges of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is the symbol designating that. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it correct that these two symbols near the Old Town and the one close to the bay, the beach, these two are different? They don't seem to be the same, at least the way they are drawn on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me one more thing: In the course of your examination-in-chief, when you were asked about the position of the artillery weapon marked by a symbol, when my learned friend was asking you about anti-aircraft weapons, when you look at the symbol, can you tell the position of that weapon vis-a-vis the symbol?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you a clarification as to the whereabouts of the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. But to avoid wasting time, my learned friend asked you, when you look at the symbol for anti-aircraft guns, when she asked you "where is the weapon," you said on the top of the symbol. So on the top of that symbol is the place where this gun was actually positioned. Is that what you explained?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one explanation. But I -- there's another explanation. I said that, for instance, when we're talking about my mortar, it is in the middle of the symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that the position of the mortar is in the middle of the area covered by the symbol?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, Mr. Negodic, in what military rule does it say that the top of the symbol for anti-aircraft guns denotes its position, whereas the middle of the symbol designating mortars indicates the position of the mortar on the map? Is there a military rule which governs this matter? Or is it something that you believe to be true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I was sure about my answer concerning artillery. However, as far as air defence is concerned and anti-aircraft weapons, I'm not sure why it is that way. I was trying to indicate where the positions were judging by the stories I heard at the command. And as far as these details are concerned, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Negodic, I understand what you said about the artillery positions and the fact that the middle of the symbol denotes the position. But I can tell you that there is no military rule that says that the top of the symbol designating anti-aircraft --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My learned friend is testifying on this issue. He is putting certain assertions to the witness without really asking a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think you're slipping into that fault, Mr. Rodic. You put it correctly the first time, but now you're trying to assert it yourself. So perhaps you better move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I made an assertion, and I asked the witness whether it was correct. And I received an affirmative answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, you didn't, Mr. Rodic. He still tells you he didn't know the position with respect to anti-aircraft weapons. You're now trying to tell him that the military rule for the depiction of anti-aircraft weapons on maps is the same as for artillery. Well, that's the only fault that I'm identifying to you on the objection of counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, is there any military rule that stipulates depiction of anti-aircraft weapons by symbols wherein the anti-aircraft gun is positioned on the top of the symbol?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I said that I am not qualified enough to answer whether that is contained in the rule or not. All I meant to say is that speaking of anti-aircraft weapons, the position of the arrow should indicate the position of the gun, especially because in this map, the position was above the tip of the arrow, and that seemed to tell me that in this case it was also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Use the indicator to show this on the map. Which position are you talking about and where is the firing position there? There are many other firing positions further up and to the left. Does the red line indicate the firing position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As you see on the map now, it is drawn in here, a large square coloured white. Above that square, on the -- on the nearest road, there is a ski lift -- a cable car, not a ski lift. And that was where this Strijela 2M was positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, how did you answer the Prosecutor so positively that the tip of the symbol denotes the position of the gun, if you were not sure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was interpreted. But I said I was sure about the artillery. And as far as anti-aircraft guns, I was not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing: In view of the position as indicated by the symbol, in view of the layout of this symbol itself, is it possible that this anti-aircraft gun was also -- could have been on the wall of the Old Town? Because the symbol seems to cross over into the Old Town, to cover the ramparts and go into the wall.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I know, sir, you would like me to tell you yes or no. But please, you seem to be leading me to confirm that just because the symbol covers part of the walls that the weapon itself could have been in the Old Town. I cannot accept that. Let me finish, please. Allow me. If I said, if I asked you before this Honourable Court to show me the firing position of the mortar to the right of this position which is not drawn in anywhere near the position where it actually was, in the same way there is a considerable difference between reality and a depiction. And I'm trying to explain to the Court again. There is no way you can explain that this gun was inside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have heard you out carefully. But, please, hear me out. We haven't yet come to the mortar. What I'm asking you is this: Reading the map, you were qualified, so I'm asking you about map reading as an artillery man. I'm not asking you whether on the 6th of December anti-aircraft weapons, whether they were there or whether they were 200 metres in front or 200 metres to the left. All I'm asking you is map reading, map reading on the basis of symbols. When you say a map of this kind, written down in this way, my question to you was: Reading the map would you say that the symbol has moved to the area across the walls and into the Old Town. Would you say that by map reading, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So we have already noted that these two symbols on the Old Town and the bay and beach are different; they differ. Is that right? The two red arrows, that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. However, as the background is black, if you look on the right, it would appear that these are the same two dots as these other ones and that the person who drew the map joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But it is a full red line, not a dotted line. And I think that that full line differs from the points. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. You can see that on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, you said you weren't sure whether on the 6th of December at the position at the Old Town, whether there was the Strijela-type weapon or the Igla weapon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When my learned colleague asked you about this second symbol, this arrow with a curved line across the arrow, your answer was that you weren't sure whether there was a Strijela position there or an Igla.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the 6th of December 1991, at any given point in time, was there the danger of the infantry, the members of the JNA, should enter from either one side or the other side into the narrow area of Dubrovnik proper, the town, as you've explained to us today?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: All the approaches, all the access roads as you've already asked me were mined on time prior to that period. There were attempts from the Strincjera side and towards the Nuncijata side of Dubrovnik. And of course, combined with an infantry and tank attack on Srdj because by taking control of Fort Srdj, if I can put it -- illustrate it this way, they would have got to the roof of our house. So on the 6th of December to the best of my knowledge, there was no infantry attack from the east. And I'm talking about the Old Town. I don't know whether you were interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 25 of your statement, the one you gave to the investigators in December 2003, you say the following: "After 8.00, we fired on both the areas at the entrance to Dubrovnik just after 0800 hours as a very small number of enemy troops were moving into these areas: As we had limited ammunition, this was at a very slow tempo. The tempo of fire was very small." So this is, according to your statement given to the investigators, and judging by that it is obvious that the enemy troops, enemy soldiers, moved forward towards both the entrances into Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Towards Dubrovnik, if you look at the map from Srdj, for example, towards the main road, the highway, you will see that it is not covered by mine fields. To the right of that, you cannot see the serpentine roads from the village of Bosanka and Zarkovica. So that is the access road, the approach road. And to this very day, the peasants, the native people of the village, go on foot and use that road going into town. However, this approach road underneath Nuncijata and Strincjera at the village of Sustjepan, there was an attempt of an infantry attack there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, in both these areas at the entrance to Dubrovnik, after 8.00 in the morning, did you open fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question is this: On the 6th of December, immediately after 8.00 a.m., did you open fire on both areas at the entrance to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. Just the entrance on the Sustjepan side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So we're going away from the Old Town again. Is that right? Running away from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: How do you mean running away from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We're always running away from the Old Town. Now you say that there was no attack either?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: There wasn't an attack. But in my statement, the one that I gave on several occasions, I don't mean my testimony in Court, but before, the statement I gave before, you can see and you have that I think at your disposal that this combat position of the 82-millimetre mortar at the Lazaret position, that I have already given an explanation and said that there was no need to open fire at this part of town that you asked me, which is the eastern approach. But that there were just four mines which come under Primic and the deputy commander Pilas picked up on the 6th of December after half past 11.00 and took them to the positions of those four mines, from that combat position. Shells, not mines.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the counsel has phrased the question to this effect: "Now you say there was no attack either." The witness never said anything to that effect, Your Honour, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was it you were referring to, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was specifically related to the statement by the witness, the one he gave to the investigators, to the effect that in Dubrovnik, there were a number of enemy soldiers moving in, and that that is why artillery -- Croatian artillery forces opened fire on both the areas of access into Dubrovnik. One access to Sustjepan and Nuncijata on the left; and to the right, the right entrance from the right-hand side from the mortar symbol on to the Lazaret position which was to be found to the right of the Old Town. The witness has now stated that this attack, this infantry attack, took place only on the left-hand side; that is to say, from the Nuncijata and Sustjepan side. So my question to him was this: Is he running away from the Old Town again, from the attack, the infantry on the right? And he spoke about that in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The paragraph in the statement to the Prosecution that you referred to was number --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 25, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that will identify your source for the purposes of Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, can you tell me what you opened fire with at the entrances to town when the enemy soldiers were moving forward? What weapons and from what positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, I have already told you, I told you two minutes ago, that we did not target the eastern approach; only the northwestern approach. And we opened fire from mortars at the Solitudo camping site.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it was the position at the Solitudo camp, camping site?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, could you tell me, then, why before the examination-in-chief when reading through your statement you didn't correct paragraph 25 and say it was incorrect, incorrectly written? Why did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, an oversight, I assume, sir. Because there was action before the 6th of December at one point - I can't remember the date - when there was an attempt at infantry attack. However, after the engineers had mined that approach road, and it is a narrow road built during the days of Austria, where the old walls are 20 to 30 metres high, it is so narrow that you can't have an armoured vehicle pass by. It would have been tantamount to suicide had the infantry gone that way. So we didn't need to target that particular approach. And of course, that might have been an oversight on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, whether the road was mined, protected before you gave your statement, is that it, was it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, it was mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, 1991. That was -- well, I can't remember the exact date, but I do know that the commander -- that we asked the commander of that theatre of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To enable entrance into town from the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: We had no need to be along this access any longer because the commander himself of the -- of Dubrovnik's defence told us that we should move as far away from the Old Town as possible so that this position at Lazaret with the four mines that were picked up on the 6th of December was not operational because we didn't feel any need to have it there. It was sufficient for us to leave those four mines for safety reasons, security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, the two mortars at the Lazaret position which were there to protect the infantry from coming in from that side into Dubrovnik was still positioned there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, these two mortars at the Lazaret position, that means to the right of the Old Town, were they with a crew, manned or not manned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, it was a joint unit, and that combat position --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I have to interrupt you. I'm sorry. We've heard all that. We know all about that. What I'm interested now --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, there was no crew. On the 6th of December at that position, there was no crew. It was not manned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how long up until the 6th of December were those mortars there at the Lazaret position? How long had they been there for?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: At the request of the commander of that unit, permission was given for him to leave them -- leave a guard there at that combat position, and it wasn't operational for some time. Commander Primic took all his men and positioned them at the SDK combat position. At about half past 11.00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question again. What I asked you was this: From the 6th of December backwards, or rather before the 6th of December, how long before the 6th of December were the mortars, the 82-millimetre mortars positioned at the Lazaret position, regardless of who was there with them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Those combat positions were in that particular locality throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were they there in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: They were placed there at the beginning of November, I believe. I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So from these mortars, since they were positioned there, was fire opened? Did they open fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. But just on a single day; that is, the day before the approach road was mined from Dubac into town, or rather towards the Belvedere Hotel, 16 shells were fired. And that combat position had 20. It spent 16. And those shells remained there until the 6th of December when they were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when were these 16 shells fired?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I think this was in the first half of November. But as I said before, I'm not quite sure of the date. It's very difficult to say after so many years have gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, these 16 shells, were they fired in a single day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say, then, that the mortar, one or several, two mortars, let's say, I apologise, two mortars at the Lazaret position, as well as two mortars at the Bogosica Park position, that they went into operation only on a single day in the month of November and nothing more than that, from October to the end of December 1991? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC [Continued]
